<description>
#### Problem

RPC clients are able to easily DoS the HTTP server due to an obligatory worker thread sleep upon authentication failure.

#### Solution

Remove the sleep.

While this allows the guess rate to increase, it also fixes the DoS vector and reduces production code.

#### History

fe98cf8dc5066368b78e9ce208118c3532598dd2 from 2010 introduced RPC authentication along with the sleep. At that point the password authentication was timing-sensitive depending on the length, so the credentials could have been brute-forced. A sleep was added to help mitigate these timing attacks (and also reduce the guess rate).

The same author then introduced `TimingResistantEqual()` in 42656ea2e552b027e174fdceab7348ffcb8245c4 / https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/2886 in 2013 to solve the timing attack once and for all (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/2838 / CVE-2013-4165). That made the sleep only serve to reduce the guess rate.

#### Severity

Low since the attack requires RPC clients to be granted network access to a node.
</description>

[2026-10-12] c:6121174379 comment by hodlinator (member):
This is in draft since I've got mixed feelings about the approach. Do we want to avoid occupying every HTTP worker at the price of vastly increasing the guess-rate?

### Rejected alternative

Been mulling over a more complex approach of:
Upon authentication failure, free up the worker, but queue a "reply"-job with a deadline which keeps enqueuing itself until it reaches the deadline and then fires off the `HTTP_UNAUTHORIZED` reply. That way we allow other jobs while still keeping the guess-rate down.
*That would solve the thread workers limit but we would probably still hit the max connections limit and end up being DoS:ed that way though.*

### Alternative under consideration

Is a responsive HTTP server more important than keeping RPC passwords secret?
Does the password authentication without the sleep take enough time that we could claim user error for choosing short passwords?
If the password is stored as plaintext, we could examine it inside `InitRPCAuthentication()` and at least warn if it seems too short/simple. *That would make it more acceptable to remove the sleep.*

Guarding against longer but flawed passwords would probably involve something like https://github.com/dropbox/zxcvbn. But adding such a dependency or dropping in an implementation seems like something that might not pay for itself if used only for RPC passwords. Maybe there's a case to be made for including it *if we use it for new wallet passphrases as well*. We probably should probably help users by at least warning against defective wallet passphrases. There was an attempt to add such checks for wallet passphrases in #17950.

Maybe it would be passable for now to:
* Remove the sleep
* Only check the RPC password *length*, and warn if too short
* Add a comment referencing #17950 in the hopes that if it is ever implemented for wallets, it can be used for RPC as well
